name: Performative Utterances
statement: Some sentences don't describe an act; uttering them is the act, like I promise or I do.
meaning: A performative utterance, or performative, is a sentence that, in being uttered in appropriate circumstances, performs an action rather than describing, reporting, or stating a fact; in saying it, one does the thing. The notion was introduced by the philosopher J. L. Austin, who contrasted performatives with constatives, utterances that describe or report and are true or false. When a person says I do at a wedding, I name this ship the Queen Elizabeth while smashing the bottle, I give and bequeath my watch to my brother in a will, or I bet you sixpence it will rain tomorrow, they are not describing an action but performing one: marrying, naming, bequeathing, betting. Because performatives do not describe facts, Austin held they are not true or false but rather happy or felicitous, or unhappy or infelicitous, depending on whether certain felicity conditions are met, such as the right person in the right circumstances following the proper procedure, with the appropriate intentions. Failures of these conditions are infelicities, which Austin sorted into misfires, where the purported act is void because a condition is unmet, as when someone without the authority tries to name a ship, and abuses, where the act comes off but is insincere, as with a promise made with no intention to keep it. Austin developed these ideas in How to Do Things with Words, his William James Lectures of 1955, published in 1962, and the notion of the performative is the seed of the broader speech act theory.
mechanism: Austin identified performatives by contrast with the assumption that the job of a declarative sentence is to state a fact that is then true or false. He noticed a class of first-person, present-tense sentences whose utterance does not report an act but constitutes one. To say I promise is to promise, to say I apologize is to apologize; the saying is the doing. Since such utterances are not descriptions, they are not assessed as true or false but as felicitous or infelicitous, and their success depends on felicity conditions: there must be an accepted conventional procedure, the right persons and circumstances, correct and complete execution, and appropriate thoughts and intentions. When these conditions fail, the utterance suffers an infelicity. Austin distinguished two broad kinds. A misfire occurs when the purported act does not come off at all because the procedure is botched or misapplied, as when a person lacking the requisite authority utters I name this ship, or a marriage is void because one party is already married; the words are spoken but no naming or marrying takes place. An abuse occurs when the act is performed but insincerely or without the appropriate follow-through, as when one promises with no intention to keep the promise. Austin also distinguished explicit performatives, which contain a performative verb in the first-person present indicative active, such as I order or I apologize, often flagged by the word hereby, from implicit or primary performatives, which lack the explicit verb, as when close the door functions as an order. Finding that constatives, too, are a kind of act and that performatives can be assessed against the facts, Austin concluded the constative-performative distinction was unstable and replaced it with the general theory of locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts.

examples.text: Saying I do at a wedding, I name this ship, or I bet performs the act rather than describing it.
A ship-naming by someone lacking authority misfires; a promise made with no intention to keep it is an abuse.
I order you to close the door is an explicit performative; close the door is an implicit one performing the same act.

variants.name: Felicity conditions
variants.text: The conditions of right person, circumstance, procedure, and intention on which a performative's success depends.

variants.name: The breakdown of the distinction
variants.text: Austin's finding that constatives are acts too, dissolving the constative-performative line into the general speech act theory.

whyItMatters: The idea of the performative utterance is J. L. Austin's seminal contribution to the philosophy of language and the origin of speech act theory and modern pragmatics. By identifying a whole class of utterances that do not describe the world but change it, that marry, name, promise, bequeath, and bet, Austin overturned the long-standing assumption that the primary function of declarative sentences is to state facts assessable as true or false, and he directed attention to what speakers do with words. His apparatus of felicity conditions, and his classification of failures into misfires and abuses, gave a precise vocabulary for analyzing how such acts succeed or fail, and his discovery that the constative-performative distinction ultimately breaks down, since even stating is a kind of act, led directly to the richer theory of locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts. The notion of the performative has had wide influence beyond philosophy, in linguistics, legal theory, and social theory, where the idea that words can constitute social realities, that saying can be doing, has proved enormously fertile. As the recognition that some utterances are actions rather than descriptions, performative utterances are a foundational idea in the study of language.

working.text: notice utterances, often first-person present tense, whose saying performs an act rather than describing one.
assess whether the right person, circumstances, procedure, and intentions are in place, not whether it is true or false.
classify a failure as a misfire, where no act comes off, or an abuse, where the act is done insincerely.

limits: The notion of the performative, though foundational, turned out to be less sharp than it first appeared, as Austin himself came to see. He found no stable criterion, grammatical or otherwise, that cleanly separates performatives from constatives: stating is itself a kind of act, so constatives are performative in a broad sense, and performatives can be evaluated for something like correctness or aptness against the facts, so they are not wholly divorced from truth. For these reasons Austin abandoned the sharp constative-performative distinction in favor of the general theory of illocutionary force, in which every utterance performs acts of several kinds. There are also questions about exactly which felicity conditions govern which acts and about how to individuate and classify the acts. Some details reward care: the essay Performative Utterances appeared later than and separately from How to Do Things with Words, the spelling and wording of examples vary across editions, and later extensions of performativity to social and political theory, while real, are best sourced beyond Austin's own texts. So performative utterances robustly show that saying can be doing, understood as a seminal but unstable category that Austin superseded with the general theory of speech acts.
misreadings: A performative utterance is not made true or false by whether the act succeeds; it is felicitous or infelicitous, and a failure is a misfire or an abuse rather than a falsehood. Performatives are not a wholly separate class from ordinary statements, since Austin found stating to be an act too and abandoned the sharp distinction. And an explicit performative verb is not required for an utterance to perform an act, since implicit performatives do so without it, so treating performatives as true or false, as sharply cut off from constatives, or as needing an explicit verb, misreads Austin's notion.
origin: J. L. Austin's notion, introduced in How to Do Things with Words (1962), of an utterance that performs an action rather than describing a fact, assessed by felicity conditions and giving rise to speech act theory.
